title: Chapter 9 — The Example Of The Americans Does Not Prove That A Democratic People Can Have No Aptitude And No Taste For Science, Literature, Or Art
paragraphs: Democratic People Can Have No Aptitude And No Taste For Science, Literature, Or Art

It must be acknowledged that among few of the civilized nations of our time have the higher sciences made less progress than in the United States, and in few have great artists, fine poets, or celebrated writers been more rare. Many Europeans, struck by this fact, have seen it as a natural and inevitable result of equality. They have supposed that if a democratic state of society and democratic institutions ever prevailed over the whole earth, the human mind would gradually see its guiding lights dim, and men would sink back into a period of darkness. To reason this way is, I think, to confuse several ideas it is important to separate and examine on their own. It is to mix up, without meaning to, what is democratic with what is merely American.

The religion professed by the first emigrants, and handed down by them to their descendants — simple in its worship, austere and almost harsh in its principles, and hostile to external symbols and ceremonial pomp — is naturally unfavorable to the fine arts, and barely tolerates the pleasures of literature. The Americans are a very old and very enlightened people who have landed on a new and boundless country, where they can spread at will, and which they can make fertile without difficulty. This situation has no parallel in the history of the world. In America, then, everyone finds opportunities, unknown elsewhere, to make or increase his fortune. The spirit of gain is always on the stretch, and the human mind, constantly turned away from the pleasures of imagination and the labors of the intellect, is governed there by no impulse but the pursuit of wealth. Manufacturing and commercial classes are to be found in the United States as in every other country, but what has never happened anywhere else is that the whole community is simultaneously engaged in productive industry and commerce. I am convinced that if the Americans had been alone in the world, with the freedom and knowledge their forefathers acquired and the passions that are their own, they would not have been slow to discover that progress cannot long be made in the application of the sciences without cultivating the theory of them, and that all the arts are perfected by one another. However absorbed they might have been by the pursuit of their main object of desire, they would soon have admitted that it is necessary to turn aside from it occasionally, in order to attain it more fully in the end.

The taste for the pleasures of the mind is, moreover, so natural to the heart of civilized man that among the polite nations least inclined to give themselves to such pursuits, a certain number of citizens always take part in them. This intellectual craving, once felt, would very soon have been satisfied. But at the very time when the Americans were naturally inclined to require of science nothing but its specific applications to the useful arts and the means of making life comfortable, learned and literary Europe was engaged in exploring the common sources of truth and in improving, at the same time, everything that can serve the pleasures or satisfy the wants of man. At the head of the enlightened nations of the Old World, the inhabitants of the United States singled out one in particular, to which they were closely united by a common origin and by kindred habits. Among this people they found distinguished men of science, skilled artists, writers of eminence, and they were able to enjoy the treasures of the intellect without having to labor to amass them. I cannot consent to separate America from Europe, in spite of the ocean that lies between. I regard the people of the United States as that portion of the English people charged with exploring the wilds of the New World, while the rest of the nation, enjoying more leisure and less harassed by the drudgery of life, can devote its energies to thought and extend in every direction the empire of the mind. The position of the Americans is therefore quite exceptional, and it may be believed that no democratic people will ever be placed in a similar one. Their strictly Puritanical origin, their exclusively commercial habits, even the country they inhabit — which seems to divert their minds from the pursuit of science, literature, and the arts — the proximity of Europe, which allows them to neglect these pursuits without relapsing into barbarism, and a thousand particular causes, of which I have only been able to point out the most important — have together fixed the mind of the American on purely practical objects. His passions, his needs, his education, and everything around him seem to unite in drawing the native of the United States earthward. His religion alone bids him turn, from time to time, a brief and distracted glance toward heaven. Let us cease, then, to view all democratic nations behind the mask of the American people, and try to see them instead in their own proper features.

It is possible to imagine a people not subdivided into castes or ranks, in which the law, recognizing no privileges, divides inherited property into equal shares, but which at the same time lacks both knowledge and freedom. Nor is this an empty hypothesis. A despot may find it in his interest to make his subjects equal and leave them ignorant, the better to keep them enslaved. Not only would a democratic people of this kind show neither aptitude nor taste for science, literature, or art, but it would probably never come into possession of them. The law of descent would on its own destroy fortunes at every succeeding generation, and no one would acquire new fortunes. The poor man, without knowledge or freedom, would not even conceive the idea of raising himself to wealth, and the rich man would allow himself to be degraded into poverty without thinking of self-defense. Between these two members of the community a complete and unshakable equality would soon be established.

No one would then have time or taste to devote himself to the pursuits or pleasures of the intellect. All men would remain paralyzed in a state of common ignorance and equal servitude. When I picture a democratic society of this kind, I imagine myself in one of those low, stuffy, gloomy rooms where the light breaking in from outside soon fails and fades. A sudden heaviness overcomes me, and I grope through the surrounding darkness for the opening that will bring me back to daylight and air.

But none of this applies to men already enlightened who retain their freedom after abolishing among themselves those peculiar and hereditary rights that perpetuated the holding of property in the hands of certain individuals or bodies. When men living in a democratic state of society are enlightened, they readily see that they are enclosed within no fixed limits forcing them to be content with their present fortune. They therefore all conceive the idea of increasing it. If they are free, they all try, but not all succeed in the same way. The legislature, it is true, no longer grants privileges, but privileges are bestowed by nature. Since natural inequality is very great, fortunes become unequal as soon as every man uses all his faculties to get rich. The law of descent prevents the establishment of wealthy families, but it does not prevent the existence of wealthy individuals. It constantly brings the members of the community back to a common level, from which they constantly escape. And the inequality of fortunes grows in proportion as knowledge is spread and liberty is increased.

A sect that arose in our time, famous for its talents and its extravagance, proposed to concentrate all property in the hands of a central power, whose task would afterwards be to parcel it out to individuals according to their capacity. This would have been a way of escaping the complete and eternal equality that seems to threaten democratic society. But it would be a simpler and less dangerous remedy to grant no privilege to anyone — giving to all equal cultivation and equal independence, and leaving everyone to determine his own position. Natural inequality will very soon make its way, and wealth will spontaneously pass into the hands of the most capable.

Free and democratic communities, then, will always contain a considerable number of people enjoying opulence or competence. The wealthy will not be as closely linked to each other as the members of the old aristocratic class were. Their tendencies will be different, and they will hardly ever enjoy leisure as secure or as complete. But they will be far more numerous than those of the old aristocratic class could ever be. These people will not be strictly confined to the cares of practical life, and they will still be able, though in different degrees, to indulge in the pursuits and pleasures of the intellect. And they will indulge in them. For if it is true that the human mind leans, on one side, toward the narrow, the practical, and the useful, it naturally rises, on the other, toward the infinite, the spiritual, and the beautiful. Physical needs confine it to the earth, but as soon as the tie is loosened, it unbends itself again.

Not only will the number of those who can take an interest in the productions of the mind be enlarged, but the taste for intellectual enjoyment will descend, step by step, even to those who in aristocratic societies seem to have neither time nor ability to indulge in it. When hereditary wealth, the privileges of rank, and the prerogatives of birth have disappeared, and when every man draws his strength from himself alone, it becomes evident that the chief cause of the difference between the fortunes of men is the mind. Whatever tends to strengthen, extend, or adorn the mind at once rises to great value. The usefulness of knowledge becomes strikingly obvious even to the eyes of the multitude; those who have no taste for its charms still set store by its results and make some effort to acquire it. In free and enlightened democratic ages, nothing separates men from each other or keeps them in their own sphere. They rise and sink with extreme rapidity. All classes live in constant contact because they are so close together. They communicate and mingle every day; they imitate and envy one another. This suggests to the people many ideas, notions, and desires they would never have entertained if the distinctions of rank had been fixed and society at rest. In such nations the servant never regards himself as a complete stranger to the pleasures and labors of his master, nor the poor man to those of the rich. The rural population becomes like that of the towns, and the provinces like the capital. No one easily allows himself to be reduced to the merely material cares of life, and the humblest artisan occasionally casts an eager and furtive glance into the higher regions of the intellect. People do not read with the same ideas or in the same way as in an aristocratic community, but the circle of readers is constantly enlarged until it takes in all the citizens.

As soon as the multitude begins to take an interest in the labors of the mind, it discovers that to excel in any of them is a powerful means of gaining fame, power, or wealth. The restless ambition produced by equality at once takes this direction, as it does all others. The number of those who cultivate science, letters, and the arts becomes immense. The intellectual world springs into prodigious activity. Everyone tries to open a path there for himself and to draw the eyes of the public after him. Something similar happens to what takes place in society in the United States, politically considered. What is done is often imperfect, but the attempts are innumerable; and although the results of individual effort are usually very small, the total is always very large.

It is therefore not true to claim that men living in democratic ages are naturally indifferent to science, literature, and the arts. The only thing that must be admitted is that they cultivate them in their own way, and bring to the task their own particular strengths and weaknesses.
